dek: VeriFone made the card terminals that sit on store counters and let merchants accept credit and debit payments.
lede: If you swiped a card at a shop counter in the 2000s, there was a good chance a VeriFone terminal read it. The company began in Honolulu in 1981 as a maker of check-verification devices, spent several years inside Hewlett-Packard, and came back out as an independent business backed by private equity. By the spring of 2005, chip cards were spreading across Europe and Asia, and every merchant on earth needed hardware that could keep up with the networks.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: The bet was simple: the moment a customer pays should be fast, cheap and trusted. Early VeriFone devices replaced the phone call a clerk made to check a card. Later models added PIN pads, receipt printers and secure software. VeriFone sold through banks and payment processors as well as directly, so its terminals spread far beyond any one retailer. The quiet strength of the business was its installed base, which turned each upgrade cycle into new orders.

sections.heading: Back on the Board
sections.body: VeriFone priced its offering at $10 a share in April 2005 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange under the fitting ticker PAY. It grew through acquisitions, most notably the purchase of Lipman Electronic Engineering in 2006, and later pushed into taxi screens and mobile payments. Competition from newer, phone-based readers squeezed the old terminal business. In 2018 Francisco Partners took the company private in a deal worth about $3.4 billion.

tagline: Fast Lane to the Options Pit
dek: optionsXpress ran an online brokerage built for individual investors who traded stock options, futures and equities.
lede: Options trading once belonged to floor traders in Chicago's crowded pits. optionsXpress, founded in that city in 2000, put the same contracts in front of ordinary investors through a web browser, with tools for pricing and strategy that had been rare outside professional desks. It filed to go public in early 2005, as online brokers recovered from the dot-com crash and a new wave of active traders went looking for cheaper, faster ways to trade.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: The founders bet that retail investors would trade options if someone made it easy and cheap. Instead of treating options as an add-on to stock trading, optionsXpress built its whole platform around them, with chains, calculators and education aimed at self-directed traders. Low flat commissions drew active customers, and the firm earned well on each account. It stayed lean and profitable, which set it apart from many brokers of its era.

sections.heading: From Pit to Portfolio
sections.body: The company priced its IPO at $16.50 a share in January 2005 and traded on Nasdaq as OXPS. It stayed profitable through the following years, added futures trading, and bought other brokerage businesses. In 2011 Charles Schwab acquired optionsXpress in a stock deal worth about $1 billion, folding its options tools and its active-trader customers into one of the largest brokers in the United States.

cover.artwork: Arrival of the Normandy Train, Gare Saint-Lazare

tagline: A Trading Floor for Phone Calls
dek: Arbinet ran an electronic exchange where telephone carriers bought and sold capacity to route international calls.
lede: Every international phone call has to pass from one carrier to another, and in the 1990s those handoffs were arranged through slow, private deals. Arbinet turned that market into an exchange. Carriers posted the routes they could offer and the prices they would pay, and Arbinet matched them, routed the traffic and settled the bills. It went public in December 2004, when voice-over-IP was cutting the cost of calls and carriers were hungry for cheap routes.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Arbinet treated phone minutes as a commodity that could be traded like any other. Its platform let a small carrier in one country reach buyers it would never meet in person, while Arbinet took on credit risk and settlement. The exchange earned fees on each minute traded. The model worked best when lots of small, nimble carriers wanted access to global routes without signing dozens of separate contracts.

sections.heading: Thin Margins, Long Lines
sections.body: Arbinet priced its shares at $17.50 in December 2004 and listed on Nasdaq. Volume on the exchange grew, but prices per minute kept falling as calling moved to the internet and mobile phones. The company spent the next years trying to add new services and cut costs. In 2011 Primus Telecommunications acquired Arbinet, ending its run as a public company.

fate: Renamed Market Leader; acquired by Trulia, 2013 ($355M)
dek: HouseValues offered free online home valuations to homeowners and sold the resulting leads to local real estate agents.
lede: In 2004 the American housing market was in full boom, and homeowners were curious about what their houses might fetch. HouseValues, based near Seattle, answered that question online. A homeowner typed in an address, and a local agent followed up with a market report. Agents paid HouseValues for those contacts. The company filed to go public that December, at the height of a market that seemed like it would only go up.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: HouseValues bet that the internet could fill an agent's pipeline better than mailers or open houses. A curious homeowner was an early sign of a future listing, and the company sold those signals to agents by territory and subscription. As the business grew it added buyer leads and tools to help agents manage contacts. Its fortunes, though, were tied tightly to how many agents were busy and willing to spend.

sections.heading: After the Boom
sections.body: The company priced its IPO at $15 a share in December 2004 and traded on Nasdaq under the ticker SOLD. When the housing market turned in 2006 and 2007, agents cut spending and revenue fell. HouseValues reworked itself into a software company for agents and renamed itself Market Leader. In 2013 Trulia bought Market Leader for about $355 million, and Zillow later acquired Trulia.

cover.theme: an old farmhouse (what is my home worth)

dek: Ninetowns sold software that let Chinese exporters and importers file inspection and quarantine paperwork electronically with the government.
lede: In 2004 China was becoming the workshop of the world, and every container leaving its ports needed paperwork. Ninetowns, based in Beijing, built software that let companies file inspection and quarantine forms online with the government agency in charge, instead of carrying stacks of paper to an office. Its American depositary shares were offered in December 2004, when investors were eager for a piece of China's growing internet and software market.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Ninetowns bet that as China's trade boomed, the state would move its customs and inspection processes onto computers. By building the software that companies used to talk to the inspection system, Ninetowns placed itself in the path of a large and growing flow of filings. Its customers were thousands of exporters who needed the tools to keep goods moving through the ports.

sections.heading: A Quiet Exit
sections.body: Ninetowns priced its ADSs at $11 in December 2004 and listed on Nasdaq under the ticker NINE. The stock fell well below its offering price in later years as the company's core business slowed and it tried new ventures. In 2012 a group of directors and officers led by chief executive Wang Shuang proposed to buy out the public shareholders. The deal closed in 2014 at $1.80 per share.

cover.theme: boats pulling oars under autumn skies (a trading nation)
cover.artwork: Pulling Oars under Clearing Autumn Skies 晴秋涉櫂圖

tagline: A Free Phone in the Mail
dek: InPhonic sold mobile phones and wireless service plans online, earning commissions from carriers for each new subscriber.
lede: In 2004 Americans were trading up to camera phones and comparing plans from a crowded field of wireless carriers. InPhonic, based in Washington, D.C., ran websites where shoppers could pick a phone and plan side by side, often getting the handset free or nearly free. Carriers paid InPhonic a commission for every new customer. The company went public in November 2004, as online shopping for big purchases was becoming normal.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: InPhonic bet that buying a phone plan, a confusing purchase full of fine print, would move online. It ran its own sites and powered stores for other brands, then used carrier commissions to subsidize cheap handsets. The model grew fast. It also depended on rebates and on customers staying with their carriers long enough for commissions to hold. Its sites became some of the largest online sellers of wireless plans in the country.

sections.heading: Rebates and Reckoning
sections.body: InPhonic priced its IPO at $19 a share in November 2004 and listed on Nasdaq. Revenue grew quickly, but losses mounted and customers complained about slow and missing rebates. Carrier payments were clawed back when subscribers cancelled early. In November 2007 InPhonic filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, and its assets were sold to a new owner soon after. Its rise and fall showed how hard it was to profit from rebates.

cover.theme: telegraphic love (a phone in the mail)

dek: MarketAxess runs an electronic trading platform where institutional investors buy and sell corporate bonds.
lede: Stocks had moved onto screens by 2004, but corporate bonds still traded mostly by telephone, one dealer at a time. MarketAxess, founded in New York in 2000, gave big investors a way to ask many dealers for prices at once and trade electronically. When it went public in November 2004, it was one of the few survivors of a crowded field of bond-trading startups from the dot-com years.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: The bet was that corporate bonds would follow stocks onto electronic markets, even though bonds are traded less often and in far more varieties. MarketAxess began by letting investors request quotes from several dealers in one step, which saved time and improved prices. Over time it added ways for investors to trade with each other, and it built data products from the trading flowing through its system.

sections.heading: A Slow Revolution
sections.body: MarketAxess priced its shares at $11 in November 2004 and listed on Nasdaq. Electronic bond trading spread steadily rather than all at once, and the company grew with it, adding high-yield, emerging-market and international bonds. It became one of the leading venues for credit trading worldwide. More than twenty years after the offering, it is still public and trades as MKTX.

tagline: A Home Page for a Community
dek: PlanetOut ran websites, magazines and travel businesses serving gay, lesbian, bisexual and transgender audiences.
lede: In the mid-1990s the web offered something many gay and lesbian people had never had: a way to find each other privately and safely. PlanetOut, founded in San Francisco, became one of the first online homes for that community. It later merged with Gay.com and added magazines such as The Advocate and Out. When it went public in October 2004, it was the largest media company aimed at LGBT readers.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: PlanetOut bet that a community underserved by mainstream media would gather online and that advertisers would follow. Its sites mixed news, personals and forums, and paid memberships became an important source of revenue. The company saw itself as a media brand for a whole audience, and it expanded into print and travel to reach that audience in more places. It also built a strong paid subscriber base among its users.

sections.heading: Turning the Page
sections.body: PlanetOut priced its IPO at $9 a share in October 2004 and listed on Nasdaq under the ticker LGBT. Growth slowed as social networks and free dating sites drew users away. The print and travel businesses also struggled, and the company sold them off. In 2009 PlanetOut combined with Here Media, ending its run as an independent public company. The brands it gathered still exist in other hands today.

dek: eCOST.com sold discounted computers, electronics and closeout goods online, with deals that ran for a limited time.
lede: eCOST.com began as part of PC Mall, a catalog seller of computers and gear, and was spun out as its own public company in August 2004. The idea was a web store built around bargains: refurbished laptops, closeout cameras and daily deals that disappeared when stock ran out. It went public at a time when online electronics shopping was growing fast but margins were famously thin.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: eCOST bet that price-hunting shoppers would come back again and again for short-lived deals. It used the buying power and warehouse of its former parent to offer a wide range of tech products at low prices. The trouble with that model is that it rewards whoever is willing to earn the least on each sale, and the field was crowded. Free shipping offers and email deals kept customers returning.

sections.heading: Short-Lived Deals
sections.body: eCOST priced its IPO at $5.80 a share in August 2004 and listed on Nasdaq. Sales grew, but losses followed and the stock fell. In early 2006 PFSweb, an e-commerce services company, completed a stock merger with eCOST. PFSweb later sold the eCOST assets back to PC Mall in 2011. The brand passed through several owners after that, while larger rivals such as Amazon and Newegg took over the market.

cover.theme: a warehouse on the wharf (bargains by the pallet)

dek: RightNow Technologies sold hosted customer-service software that helped companies answer questions by web, email and phone.
lede: RightNow was a software company from Bozeman, Montana, far from Silicon Valley. Greg Gianforte started it in 1997 to help companies handle customer questions online. Its software was hosted and sold by subscription, years before that became the standard way to buy business software. When RightNow filed to go public in the summer of 2004, the idea of renting software over the internet was still unproven to many investors.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: RightNow bet that companies would rather rent customer-service software than install it themselves. Its first product was a searchable knowledge base that let customers find answers without calling. It then added email handling, call-center tools and feedback surveys. The company built a large base of customers, including government agencies and big consumer brands, from its office in the mountains. Its success helped turn Bozeman into a small hub for software work.

sections.heading: From Bozeman to Redwood
sections.body: RightNow priced its IPO at $7 a share in August 2004 and listed on Nasdaq. Its timing proved good, as software-as-a-service took off over the following years. Revenue grew steadily, and the company became one of the better-known names in customer-service software. Oracle agreed to buy RightNow in 2011 for about $1.5 billion and closed the deal in early 2012.

cover.theme: a boy holding an hourglass (right now)
cover.artwork: Boy Holding Hourglass and Chinese Fan

dek: Greenfield Online ran online survey panels for market researchers and later owned the European shopping comparison site Ciao.
lede: Market research once meant phone calls during dinner and clipboards in shopping malls. Greenfield Online, based in Wilton, Connecticut, moved surveys onto the internet, building large panels of people who agreed to answer questions online. Research firms and brands paid for the responses. When the company went public in July 2004, it had also bought Ciao, a European site where shoppers compared prices and wrote reviews.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Greenfield bet that the internet would make surveys faster and cheaper than any phone bank. A large, well-profiled online panel let researchers reach the right people in days instead of weeks. The Ciao purchase added a second business built on consumer opinion, with revenue from shopping referrals and its own survey community in Europe. Survey panels became the standard tool of the market research trade in the years that followed.

sections.heading: The Ciao Prize
sections.body: Greenfield Online priced its IPO at $13 a share in July 2004 and listed on Nasdaq under the ticker SRVY. The Ciao business grew into a major part of the company. In 2008 Microsoft agreed to buy Greenfield for about $486 million, mainly to add Ciao to its search and shopping efforts in Europe. Microsoft later sold the survey business.

fate: Taken private by Bain Capital and partners, 2017 ($500M)
dek: Blue Nile sold diamonds, engagement rings and fine jewelry online, with detailed grading data for each stone.
lede: Few people expected the internet to sell engagement rings. Diamonds were costly, emotional purchases, and they were sold in hushed jewelry stores with heavy markups. Blue Nile, founded in Seattle in 1999, put thousands of certified diamonds online with their cut, color, clarity and carat listed in plain view. When it went public in May 2004, it had shown that careful buyers would spend thousands of dollars on a ring they had only seen on a screen.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Blue Nile bet that information would beat atmosphere. By listing grading reports and prices openly, it let shoppers compare stones the way they compared other goods. It did not hold most of its diamonds in inventory. Instead it listed stones held by suppliers, which kept costs low and let it charge far less than a typical store. Its return policy and certified grading gave buyers the confidence to spend.

sections.heading: Beyond the Screen
sections.body: Blue Nile priced its IPO at $20.50 a share in May 2004 and listed on Nasdaq under the ticker NILE. The stock rose sharply on its first day. Blue Nile became the best-known online jeweler in America and expanded abroad. In 2017 a group led by Bain Capital took the company private for about $500 million, and it later opened physical showrooms.

cover.theme: the Jewel River of Plovers (jewels and water)
cover.artwork: The Jewel River of Plovers (Chidori no Tamagawa), from an untitled series of Six Jewel Rivers

dek: TOM Online was a Chinese internet portal that earned most of its money from ringtones, games and text messages on mobile phones.
lede: In early 2004 China had more mobile phones than any other country, and most people went online through them. TOM Online, part of the Hong Kong conglomerate TOM Group, ran a web portal but earned most of its money from wireless services: ringtones, pictures, games and text message alerts sold through China Mobile. It listed in New York and Hong Kong in March 2004, in the middle of a rush of Chinese internet offerings.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: TOM Online bet that Chinese users would pay small amounts, over and over, for content on their phones. The carriers collected the fees and passed a share back. The model could grow quickly, but it depended on the rules set by the carriers, who could change billing policies with little warning. Many Chinese internet companies of the time depended on the same kind of mobile revenue.

sections.heading: Back to the Parent
sections.body: TOM Online priced its shares at the equivalent of about $15.55 per ADS in March 2004 and traded on Nasdaq and the Hong Kong exchange. Changes in China Mobile's billing rules hit the wireless business hard over the next few years. In 2007 the parent company, TOM Group, bought out the minority shareholders and took TOM Online private. Its story marks a brief era when phone carriers decided which content companies thrived in China.

dek: Provide Commerce ran ProFlowers, which shipped fresh flowers to customers directly from growers instead of through local florists.
lede: In the late 1990s most flowers sent across the country passed through a wire service and a local florist, often sitting in coolers for days. Jared Polis, a young internet entrepreneur, founded ProFlowers in 1998 on a different plan: take the order online and ship the stems in a box straight from the farm. By the time its parent, Provide Commerce, went public in December 2003, ProFlowers had become one of the largest flower sellers online.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: The bet was that cutting out the middle of the supply chain would mean fresher flowers and lower prices. ProFlowers carried almost no inventory. Growers packed and shipped orders directly, coordinated by Provide Commerce's software. The company later applied the same model to other perishables, including gourmet foods and fruit, and bought rival gift sellers. Seasonal peaks were steep, and the software had to scale for a few huge days each year.

sections.heading: Petals and Profits
sections.body: Provide Commerce priced its IPO at $15 a share in December 2003 and listed on Nasdaq. The company grew around big gift holidays such as Valentine's Day and Mother's Day, and it expanded through acquisitions. In 2006 Liberty Media bought Provide Commerce for about $477 million. Jared Polis went on to a career in politics. The ProFlowers brand continued under later owners for many years.

fate: Taken private by Carlyle and Providence, 2007; later acquired by Fiserv, 2013
tagline: The Engine Room of Small Banks
dek: Open Solutions sold core processing software that community banks and credit unions used to run accounts and transactions.
lede: Every bank needs a core system: the software that keeps track of deposits, loans and every transaction. Large banks built their own or bought from a few giant vendors. Open Solutions, based in Glastonbury, Connecticut, focused on community banks and credit unions, offering modern software built on open, standard databases. It went public in November 2003, as smaller banks were replacing aging systems to compete online with bigger rivals.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Open Solutions bet that smaller banks wanted the same kind of flexible, modern technology as the giants. Its core platform used a single shared database, which made it easier for banks to add new products and connect other software. The company grew by winning new banks and by buying other vendors that served the same market. Its customers tended to stay for years, since replacing a bank's core system is slow and risky.

sections.heading: Into Larger Hands
sections.body: Open Solutions priced its IPO at $17 a share in November 2003 and listed on Nasdaq. It continued to buy smaller companies to widen its offering. In 2007 the private equity firms Carlyle Group and Providence Equity Partners took Open Solutions private. Fiserv, one of the largest providers of bank technology, acquired the company in 2013. Its software kept running inside many small banks and credit unions.

cover.artwork: Young Woman at an Open Half-Door

fate: Bankrupt, 2008; brand sold to Provide Commerce
dek: RedEnvelope sold curated, upscale gifts online and by catalog, delivered in its signature red box.
lede: RedEnvelope began in the late 1990s as an online gift shop and grew into a brand known for its red packaging and hand-picked selection. The pitch was taste and convenience: a store that did the choosing for you and shipped the gift wrapped. It went public in September 2003, a cautious time for e-commerce offerings, as one of the few online retailers willing to test the market after the crash.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: RedEnvelope bet that busy shoppers would pay for a well-edited gift and a strong brand. It sold a mix of engraved keepsakes, home goods and holiday items, many of them exclusive. Catalogs drove much of its traffic. The business, though, was heavily seasonal, with a large share of each year's sales landing in the weeks before Christmas. Free gift wrapping and personalized items set it apart from larger stores.

sections.heading: The Last Delivery
sections.body: RedEnvelope priced its IPO at $14 a share in September 2003 and listed on Nasdaq. It struggled to turn a steady profit as marketing and shipping costs stayed high. In 2008 the company filed for bankruptcy. Provide Commerce, the parent of ProFlowers, bought the RedEnvelope brand and assets. The RedEnvelope name lived on as a gift brand under its new owner, sold alongside flowers and other gifts.

cover.theme: a decorated envelope with hibiscus (a gift)

dek: iPass gave business travelers one account to get online through dial-up numbers, hotel networks and Wi-Fi hotspots around the world.
lede: Before smartphones and free Wi-Fi, a business traveler's laptop was only as useful as the next phone jack. iPass built a global network of access points by striking deals with hundreds of internet providers, then sold companies one simple account that worked almost anywhere. Its software found a local connection and handled billing behind the scenes. iPass went public in July 2003, one of the first tech offerings to do well after the crash.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: iPass bet that it could stitch together other companies' networks into one service and sell it to corporate IT departments. It owned little infrastructure of its own. Its value lay in the agreements, the client software and the security that made remote access safe for large employers. As travelers moved from dial-up to hotel broadband and Wi-Fi, iPass followed them. Large corporations signed on to give their whole traveling workforce one way to connect.

sections.heading: A Long Way From Dial-Up
sections.body: iPass priced its IPO at $14 a share in July 2003 and listed on Nasdaq. The shares rose strongly at first. Over the next decade, free Wi-Fi and mobile data eroded the need for its service, and the company shifted toward Wi-Fi software and data. Pareteum, a telecom software company, acquired iPass in early 2019. By then, its original dial-up service was a memory.

cover.artwork: Nissaka: Sayo Mountain Pass (Nissaka, Sayo no nakayama), from the series "Fifty-three Stations of the Tokaido (Tokaido gojusan tsugi no uchi)," also known as the Hoeido Tokaido

tagline: A Front Door for the Company
dek: Plumtree Software sold corporate portal software that gathered a company's applications and documents into one personalized web page.
lede: In the late 1990s, people at work had to hunt across dozens of systems for the information they needed. Plumtree, founded in San Francisco, offered a single web page for each employee, built from small windows called portlets that drew data from many sources. The idea borrowed from consumer portals like My Yahoo and brought it inside the firewall. Plumtree went public in June 2002, a difficult moment for any technology offering.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Plumtree bet that companies would want one front door to all their software. Its portal could pull in content from different vendors, so large organizations with mixed systems found it useful. Big customers, including government agencies, adopted it widely. Co-founder Glenn Kelman later became the chief executive of Redfin. Its portals often became the internal home page that thousands of employees saw each morning.

sections.heading: Bought by a Bigger Player
sections.body: Plumtree priced its IPO at $8.50 a share in June 2002 and listed on Nasdaq. It was one of very few software companies to go public that year, and it grew modestly as the economy recovered. Larger vendors began bundling portals with their own platforms. In 2005 BEA Systems acquired Plumtree for about $200 million. BEA folded Plumtree into its own portal products, and Oracle later bought BEA.

fate: Still public as Beyond, Inc. (NYSE: BYON)
dek: Overstock.com sold surplus and closeout goods online, and later grew into a large online seller of furniture and home goods.
lede: When the dot-com crash left warehouses full of unsold goods, Overstock.com was ready to buy them. Founded in 1999 by Patrick Byrne in Salt Lake City, the company sold excess inventory from other retailers and manufacturers at deep discounts. By the time it went public in May 2002, through an unusual Dutch auction offering, it had become one of the better-known bargain sites on the web.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Overstock bet that the internet was the ideal place to clear surplus stock. Liquidation had always been a messy business of brokers and outlet stores. A single website could reach millions of bargain hunters at once. Over time the company shifted from pure closeouts toward new home furnishings, where it found steadier supply and better margins. Its quirky ads and low prices made it a household name.

sections.heading: Many Lives After the Auction
sections.body: Overstock priced its offering at $13 a share in May 2002 and listed on Nasdaq. The company became known for its outspoken founder, its campaigns against short sellers, and an early push into blockchain projects. Byrne left in 2019. In 2023 the company bought the Bed Bath & Beyond brand, renamed itself Beyond, Inc., and continues to trade publicly. Its path from closeouts to home goods is one of the longer stories in American e-commerce.

dek: Netflix began by mailing DVD rentals with no late fees, then became the world's largest subscription streaming service.
lede: In 2002 most Americans rented movies from a video store and paid late fees when they forgot to return them. Netflix offered a monthly subscription instead. Customers built a queue on the website, and red envelopes carrying DVDs arrived in the mail. Founded in 1997 by Reed Hastings and Marc Randolph, the company had several hundred thousand subscribers when it went public in May 2002. Many investors still doubted it could survive against Blockbuster.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Netflix bet on two things. The first was that the cheap, light DVD could travel by mail. The second was that a subscription with no late fees would win customers' loyalty. Its recommendation engine helped people find older films they had never heard of, which made the large catalog valuable. From the start, the founders talked about one day delivering movies over the internet.

sections.heading: From Mailbox to Stream
sections.body: Netflix priced its IPO at $15 a share in May 2002 and listed on Nasdaq. It began streaming in 2007, started producing original series in 2013, and expanded to nearly every country in the world. Blockbuster went bankrupt in 2010. Netflix is still public and trades as NFLX, and it is now one of the most valuable media companies on earth.

dek: BAM! Entertainment published video games, many of them based on licensed cartoons, films and sports brands.
lede: At the turn of the millennium, a new generation of consoles was arriving: the PlayStation 2, Xbox, GameCube and Game Boy Advance. BAM! Entertainment, founded in San Jose in 1999 by Ray Musci, set out to publish games for all of them, often using well-known licensed characters. It went public in November 2001, only weeks after the September 11 attacks, in one of the quietest markets for new offerings in years.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: BAM bet that familiar brands would help a young publisher stand out on crowded store shelves. It signed licenses for cartoon and movie properties and paid outside studios to build the games. That approach let it release titles quickly. It also meant paying large sums up front for licenses, with no guarantee the games would sell. It released games for nearly every major console and handheld of the period.

sections.heading: Game Over
sections.body: BAM priced its IPO at $8 a share in November 2001 and listed on Nasdaq. Several of its games sold poorly, and the costs of licenses and development outran revenue. The company cut staff, sold and later bought back a London studio, and was delisted from Nasdaq. It continued releasing a few titles until 2005, when it went out of business after a bankruptcy filing.

cover.artwork: Fireworks at Ryōgoku  (Ryōgoku  hanabi), from the series One Hundred Famous Views of Edo (Meisho Edo hyakkei)

fate: Still public as Bread Financial (NYSE: BFH)
dek: Alliance Data Systems ran loyalty programs, store-branded credit cards and transaction processing for large retailers.
lede: Alliance Data was assembled in 1996 when the investment firm Welsh, Carson, Anderson & Stowe combined a retail credit card bank with a transaction processing business. It added the Air Miles loyalty program in Canada soon after. By June 2001, when it went public, it was a quiet giant behind the store credit cards and rewards programs used by millions of shoppers. The offering came in a weak market, months after the dot-com crash.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Alliance Data bet that retailers would hand off their loyalty and credit card programs to a specialist. Store cards and rewards programs generated detailed data about what customers bought. Alliance Data used that data to help retailers market more precisely, while earning interest and fees on the cards it issued. It later added the Epsilon marketing business. Its programs reached millions of households through familiar store brands.

sections.heading: Breaking Into Pieces
sections.body: Alliance Data priced its IPO at $12 a share in June 2001 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange. It grew for years through acquisitions and became a member of the S&P 500. In the late 2010s it sold Epsilon and spun off its loyalty business. In 2022 the remaining card business renamed itself Bread Financial. Bread Financial is still public and trades on the New York Stock Exchange.

cover.artwork: A Study for the Card Players

dek: Instinet ran one of the first electronic trading networks, letting institutions and later others trade stocks directly by computer.
lede: Instinet was electronic trading before most people had heard of it. Founded in 1969, it let big institutions trade stocks with each other on computer terminals, without a floor broker. Reuters bought it in 1987. By the late 1990s Instinet and newer rivals were taking a large share of Nasdaq trading. In May 2001 Reuters sold part of Instinet to the public, and a year later Instinet bought Island, an upstart rival.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Instinet bet that buyers and sellers could find each other directly through a screen and save on costs. It offered anonymity, which mattered to large investors who did not want to tip off the market. It also let institutions trade outside normal exchange hours. The model shaped what later became the standard for modern equity markets. Many of today's trading venues follow the path it opened.

sections.heading: Absorbed by the Exchange
sections.body: Instinet priced its IPO at $14.50 a share in May 2001 and listed on Nasdaq. Competition from other electronic networks and falling trading fees squeezed it. In 2005 Nasdaq agreed to buy Instinet Group for about $1.9 billion, keeping its electronic marketplace. The Instinet brokerage arm was sold to the private equity firm Silver Lake and later to Nomura. Its offering came during a long shift from trading floors to computers.

cover.artwork: Chicago Stock Exchange Trading Room: Reconstruction at the Art Institute of Chicago

dek: Riverstone Networks made high-speed routers and switches for carriers building metropolitan Ethernet networks.
lede: Riverstone was spun out of Cabletron Systems, a networking hardware company, as it broke itself into smaller units. Riverstone made routers designed for metropolitan networks, which linked offices and data centers across a city. In early 2001, telecom carriers still planned huge network buildouts, and Riverstone's equipment was aimed squarely at them. It went public in February 2001, as the market for new telecom gear was beginning to fall apart.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Riverstone bet that carriers would use Ethernet, the cheap and familiar technology of office networks, to carry traffic across cities. Its routers combined high speed with controls that let carriers sell different levels of service. The technology was sound. Its customers, though, were the same young carriers that had borrowed heavily to build networks. Its main customers were the young, competitive carriers of the late 1990s.

sections.heading: When the Carriers Fell
sections.body: Riverstone priced its IPO at $12 a share in February 2001 and listed on Nasdaq. Within months, many of its carrier customers cut spending or went bankrupt. The company later faced an accounting investigation and restated its results. In 2006 Riverstone filed for bankruptcy, and Lucent Technologies bought most of its assets. Its brief life tracked the rise and fall of the telecom boom almost exactly.

tagline: A Chip That Changed Its Mind
dek: Transmeta designed low-power processors for laptops that used software to translate standard x86 instructions on the fly.
lede: Transmeta worked in near-total secrecy for five years, and its hiring of Linux creator Linus Torvalds only added to the mystery. When it revealed the Crusoe processor in 2000, the idea was striking: a simple, power-saving chip that used software to act like an Intel processor. It promised thin laptops with long battery life. The company went public in November 2000, one of the last big hardware offerings of the boom.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Transmeta bet that it could beat Intel on power use by moving complexity from hardware into software. Its code morphing layer translated programs as they ran, which let the hardware stay small and cool. Some Japanese laptop makers adopted Crusoe. Performance, though, lagged behind expectations, and Intel answered with its own power-saving chips. Its approach was technically bold, and engineers still study it.

sections.heading: Licensing the Ideas
sections.body: Transmeta priced its IPO at $21 a share in November 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. The shares rose sharply on the first day, then fell for years as chip sales stayed small. The company shifted toward licensing its power-saving technology, and it won a large patent settlement from Intel. In 2009 Novafora acquired Transmeta. Its ideas about saving power, though, found their way into the wider industry.

cover.artwork: Three Caterpillars, a Moth, and Four Butterflies, from Diversae Insectorum...Figurae

dek: Synplicity sold software that turned written hardware descriptions into circuit designs for programmable chips.
lede: Chip designers in the 1990s increasingly described circuits in code rather than drawing them gate by gate. Synthesis software turned that code into a real design. Synplicity, based in Sunnyvale, built fast synthesis tools for programmable chips known as FPGAs, which engineers could configure after manufacturing. It went public in October 2000, as the chip industry was enjoying a record year and demand for design tools was high.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Synplicity bet that FPGAs would grow from prototyping tools into chips used in real products, and that their designers would want specialized software. Its tools were quick and worked with chips from many vendors, which gave engineers a neutral choice. The company later added tools for verifying and prototyping larger custom chips. Many hardware engineers came to rely on its tools in their daily design work.

sections.heading: Folded Into a Giant
sections.body: Synplicity priced its IPO at $8 a share in October 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. The chip downturn of 2001 slowed its growth, but the company stayed focused and kept a loyal base of engineers. In 2008 Synopsys, one of the largest chip design software companies, acquired Synplicity and added its tools to its own line. Programmable chips went on to become a large and important market, much as Synplicity had expected.

tagline: Riding the Top of the Wave
dek: CoSine Communications made network equipment that let telecom carriers sell managed security and private network services.
lede: CoSine Communications was one of the most hyped networking startups of the boom. It built large systems for telecom carriers that let them offer business customers firewalls and private networks from inside the carrier's own network. When it went public in September 2000, near the very top of the telecom bubble, its shares jumped sharply on the first day of trading.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: CoSine bet that carriers would sell security and networking as services, so that businesses would not need to buy and run their own equipment. Its systems let one carrier serve many customers from shared hardware. The idea anticipated later cloud services. It depended, though, on carriers with money to spend on new equipment. Large carriers in the United States and abroad tested its systems.

sections.heading: After the Wave Broke
sections.body: CoSine priced its IPO at $23 a share in September 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. Months later, the telecom market collapsed, and carriers stopped buying. Revenue never came close to the expectations set at the offering. In 2004 the company wound down its operations, and the remaining shell kept its cash. Its story became a symbol of how quickly the telecom boom turned to bust.

cover.artwork: Awa Province: Naruto Whirlpools (Awa, Naruto no fuha), from the series "Famous Places in the Sixty-odd Provinces (Rokujuyoshu meisho zue)"

tagline: Radio Parts for the Wireless Age
dek: WJ Communications made radio frequency chips and components for wireless base stations and broadband networks.
lede: WJ Communications grew out of Watkins-Johnson, a Silicon Valley electronics firm founded in 1957 that built microwave and defense equipment. By 2000, after a recapitalization led by the private equity firm Fox Paine, the company had refocused on radio frequency parts for the booming wireless industry. It went public in August 2000, when phone carriers were racing to build networks and RF chips were in high demand.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: WJ bet that the wireless build-out would need large numbers of high-performance amplifiers and mixers. Its parts sat inside the base stations that carried mobile calls and in broadband equipment. The company had decades of RF know-how from its parent. Its fortunes, though, depended on the spending cycles of a few big equipment makers. Its engineering roots reached back more than forty years.

sections.heading: A Long Fade
sections.body: WJ priced its IPO at $16 a share in August 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. Within a year, the telecom slump cut orders sharply. The company shrank, moved to an outsourced manufacturing model and kept selling RF parts to a narrower market. In 2008 TriQuint Semiconductor acquired WJ Communications. The deal brought its RF know-how into a larger chip company focused on wireless and networking.

cover.theme: a signal tower on a mountain (radio)
cover.artwork: Signal Tower on Elk Mountain, Maryland

dek: PeoplePC bundled a home computer with internet access for a single monthly fee, often through deals with large employers.
lede: In 1999 many American households still did not own a computer. PeoplePC, founded in San Francisco that year, offered a new PC, internet service and support for one monthly payment, like a phone plan. Its biggest moment came in 2000, when Ford and Delta Air Lines announced they would give home computers to their employees through PeoplePC. The company went public in August 2000.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: PeoplePC bet that the cost of a computer was the main barrier to getting online, and that spreading it out monthly would bring in new users. Corporate programs gave it a fast way to reach hundreds of thousands of households. The model, though, carried heavy hardware costs up front and relied on customers staying for years. It also sold through partners outside the United States.

sections.heading: Absorbed by an ISP
sections.body: PeoplePC priced its IPO at $10 a share in August 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. The stock dropped quickly as the market turned and losses grew. The company cut back the hardware offer and focused on low-cost internet access. In 2002 EarthLink acquired PeoplePC, and the brand lived on for years as a budget internet service. Its early idea, a computer paid for monthly, later returned in phone plans.

cover.theme: a crowd of people in a park
cover.artwork: A Sunday on La Grande Jatte — 1884

dek: Equinix builds and runs data centers where networks, cloud providers and companies connect their equipment to each other.
lede: The internet is made of many separate networks, and they need neutral places to connect. Equinix, founded in 1998 by Jay Adelson and Al Avery, built those meeting points: secure buildings where carriers, content companies and businesses could rent space and link their equipment directly. Its name nods to equality and exchange. Equinix went public in August 2000, a few months after the market peak, with only a handful of sites open.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Equinix bet that neutrality was the product. Because it was not a carrier itself, competing networks were willing to meet inside its buildings. Each new customer made the site more valuable to the next, since there were more partners to connect with. The idea took years and large amounts of capital to prove. Its buildings became key points where the internet's networks join.

sections.heading: Through the Bust, Around the World
sections.body: Equinix priced its IPO at $12 a share in August 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. The telecom crash nearly sank it, and the company survived through a restructuring and a merger with assets from rivals. It then grew steadily into a worldwide network of data centers and became a real estate investment trust in 2015. It is still public and trades as EQIX.

dek: America Online Latin America offered AOL's internet service in Brazil, Mexico, Argentina and Puerto Rico.
lede: By 2000 America Online had brought tens of millions of Americans online, and it wanted to repeat the feat in Latin America. It formed a joint venture with the Cisneros Group, a Venezuelan media family, to launch AOL in Brazil, Mexico and Argentina. The venture went public in August 2000, when internet stocks were already falling, with plans to spend heavily on marketing and free trial discs.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: AOL Latin America bet that AOL's easy software and brand would win in markets where few people were online yet. It localized content and spent heavily on promotions. Local rivals, however, offered free internet access, and many users were reluctant to pay a monthly fee. Phone and broadband companies also began bundling their own access. Its parent companies kept funding it for years in the hope of a turnaround.

sections.heading: Lights Out
sections.body: AOL Latin America priced its IPO at $8 a share in August 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. Subscribers grew, but losses were large and constant, and it relied on funding from its parents. Its share price sank as rival free and broadband services spread. In 2005 the company filed for bankruptcy and wound down its service. Its rise and fall marked the end of AOL's global dial-up ambitions.

dek: WebEx sold web conferencing services that let people share screens, slides and video in online meetings.
lede: In 2000, sharing a presentation with colleagues in another city usually meant a plane ticket or a fuzzy phone call. WebEx, founded by Subrah Iyar and Min Zhu, let people join a meeting in a web browser and see the same screen. It ran the service on its own global network and sold it by subscription. WebEx went public in July 2000, as the dot-com market wobbled, but its product kept selling.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: WebEx bet that companies would pay to meet online, and that the service should be hosted rather than installed. That made it an early software-as-a-service business. It built its own network to keep meetings fast and reliable. After the September 11 attacks, when many businesses cut back on travel, demand for online meetings grew quickly. Sales teams were early adopters, using it to give demonstrations to customers far away.

sections.heading: Acquired by the Network
sections.body: WebEx priced its IPO at $14 a share in July 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. It turned profitable and became the leading name in web conferencing. In 2007 Cisco bought WebEx for about $3.2 billion. Under Cisco, Webex became the core of its collaboration business, and its use surged during the pandemic of 2020. The product name is still in wide use today.

fate: Renamed Raindance; acquired by West Corporation, 2006
dek: Evoke Communications provided conference calling and web-based meeting services for businesses.
lede: Evoke Communications, based near Boulder, Colorado, sold conference calls and online meetings to businesses at a time when both were moving from operators and switchboards to the web. Customers could set up a call themselves, share slides, and invite others without help. Evoke went public in July 2000, in the same busy month as its rival WebEx, while the market for online collaboration was still young.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Evoke bet that conferencing would become a self-service product. Its system let users schedule and run their own calls and add web presentations, cutting the cost of each meeting. It sold to companies large and small. The business depended heavily on voice minutes, a market where prices kept falling. Its rival WebEx focused more on web sharing, while Evoke leaned on voice. Both were betting that meetings would move away from conference rooms.

sections.heading: A New Name, a New Owner
sections.body: Evoke priced its IPO at $8 a share in July 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. In 2001 it renamed itself Raindance Communications and focused on its business conferencing services. Raindance stayed public for several more years. In 2006 West Corporation, a large provider of call services, acquired Raindance. Conference calling remained a large business, but one dominated by bigger players with their own networks.

cover.theme: a single voice singing at sunrise

dek: Support.com sold software and services that helped companies and consumers fix computer problems remotely.
lede: When home and office computers broke in 2000, people called a help desk and waited. Support.com, based in Redwood City, built software that let companies diagnose and fix problems automatically or remotely. Its tools could check a computer's settings and repair common faults without a technician on site. It went public in July 2000, as companies were spending heavily on support for a fast-growing number of PCs.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Support.com bet that much of tech support could be automated. Its software sat on users' machines and connected back to a company's help desk, which cut the number of calls and visits. The company first sold to large corporations. It later shifted to offering remote help services directly to consumers and through partners. Its customers included large technology companies and internet providers.

sections.heading: Many Turns
sections.body: Support.com priced its IPO at $14 a share in July 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. It renamed itself SupportSoft for several years before returning to the Support.com name. The company moved from enterprise software into consumer tech support and outsourced customer service. In 2021 it merged with Greenidge Generation, a bitcoin mining company. The deal ended its long run as a tech support company.

cover.artwork: Aeneas Rescuing Anchises from Burning Troy

dek: Network Engines built compact servers and appliances that other technology companies sold under their own brands.
lede: In 2000, companies were filling data centers with servers as fast as they could, and space was expensive. Network Engines, based outside Boston, built thin, dense servers that packed more computing into each rack. It went public in July 2000, at a time when data center space was scarce and the companies building websites seemed to have unlimited budgets. Its servers were built for speed, density and reliability.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Network Engines first bet that web companies would want dense, reliable servers for their growing data centers. When that market fell away, it changed course. It began building ready-to-ship appliances for software makers, who loaded their own programs and sold the boxes under their own names. That shift gave it a steadier business. Security and storage software companies became its main customers.

sections.heading: A New Engine
sections.body: Network Engines priced its IPO at $17 a share in July 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. Its shares fell sharply after the dot-com crash as web company customers vanished. The appliance business kept the company going for another decade. In 2012 Unicom Systems acquired Network Engines. Through all its changes, it stayed based outside Boston. Its story shows how a hardware company can survive by finding a new kind of customer after its first market disappears.

cover.artwork: Picture of the Steam Engine Railway in Yatsuyama, Tokyo (Tokyo Yatsuyama shita kaigan jokisha tetsudo no zu)

dek: I-many sold software that helped drug makers and other manufacturers manage contracts, rebates and pricing agreements.
lede: Drug makers sign thousands of contracts with wholesalers, hospitals, pharmacies and insurers, each with its own rebates and price terms. Tracking all of it on spreadsheets led to errors and lost money. I-many built software to manage those contracts and calculate what was owed. It went public in July 2000, as the business software market was still hot. Investors saw contract software as a fast-growing niche.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: I-many bet that contract management in health care was complex enough to need its own software. Its products tracked prices, rebates and compliance across many trading partners. Its customers were mainly pharmaceutical and life sciences firms. The company later tried to widen its market to other industries. Its tools helped clients find money they were owed and avoid paying rebates twice. That made the value of the software easy to measure for finance teams.

sections.heading: Back to Private
sections.body: I-many priced its IPO at $9 a share in July 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. Growth slowed after the dot-com crash and the company posted repeated losses. It kept a loyal base of pharmaceutical customers. In 2009 the private equity firm LLR Partners acquired I-many for about $55 million. The deal ended its time as a public company. The business continued under private ownership, still serving drug makers and other life sciences firms.

cover.artwork: Flock of Sheep at the Edge of a Wood

dek: Sunrise Telecom made test equipment that telephone and cable companies used to check and repair their networks.
lede: Every telephone and cable network needs technicians who can test lines, find faults and confirm service is working. Sunrise Telecom, based in San Jose, built handheld and rack-mounted testers for that work. In 2000, carriers were building new networks across the country, and test gear was in demand. Sunrise Telecom went public in July 2000, when telecom equipment stocks were still near their highs.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Sunrise bet that each new network technology would need new tools to test it, from older digital phone lines to DSL, fiber and cable. It built a broad range of instruments and sold them to carriers and equipment makers. The work was steady but tied closely to how much carriers chose to spend. Its testers were used both in labs and in the field.

sections.heading: A Long Afternoon
sections.body: Sunrise Telecom priced its IPO at $15 a share in July 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. Carrier spending fell sharply the next year. In 2005 Nasdaq delisted the company after it failed to file reports during an internal investigation, and it moved to the over-the-counter market. In 2013 VeEX bought most of its operating assets. Its products lived on under the new owner.

cover.artwork: View of Mount Fuji at sunrise on New Year's Day

dek: Virage made software that indexed video so that people could search it by words spoken, faces seen and scenes shown.
lede: In 2000, video was spreading online, but it was nearly impossible to search. A news archive might hold thousands of hours of tape with only a few written notes. Virage, based in San Mateo, built software that watched and listened to video, logged the speech and scenes, and made the footage searchable like text. It went public in June 2000, just as media companies began moving archives to the web.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Virage bet that video would become as searchable as documents. Its software combined speech recognition, face recognition and scene detection to create an index of each clip. Broadcasters, government agencies and corporations used it to find footage quickly. The market for such tools grew more slowly than the company hoped. It also offered hosted services that let websites publish and search video clips.

sections.heading: A Turn in the Road
sections.body: Virage priced its IPO at $11 a share in June 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. Like many young software companies, it struggled as tech spending fell after 2001. In 2003 Autonomy, the British search software company, bought Virage and added its video tools to its own products. Its ideas about video search were early, and later services built on them at a much larger scale.

dek: Click Commerce sold software that helped manufacturers manage sales through their networks of dealers, distributors and partners.
lede: Many manufacturers do not sell directly to customers. They sell through dealers and distributors, and coordinating that network is hard. Click Commerce, based in Chicago, built web software that linked manufacturers with their partners for ordering, pricing and support. It went public in June 2000, at the peak of excitement over business-to-business commerce on the internet. The company was one of several Chicago tech firms to list in that period.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Click Commerce bet that manufacturers would move their partner relationships onto the web. Its software gave dealers a single place to check prices, place orders and get information. After the dot-com crash, the company bought other software businesses, including tools for research institutions and health care, and became steadily profitable. Its customers included large manufacturers of equipment and vehicles. Its software ran large parts of their dealer networks.

sections.heading: Home in Chicago
sections.body: Click Commerce priced its IPO at $10 a share in June 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. The shares collapsed after the bubble burst, but the company rebuilt itself through acquisitions and a tight focus on profits. In 2006 Illinois Tool Works, another Chicago-area company, bought Click Commerce. The deal gave ITW a profitable software business. It also gave Click Commerce shareholders a better outcome than most of their peers from the class of 2000.

cover.artwork: Chicago River from Rush Street Bridge, No. 188 from the series "Views of Chicago"

dek: Centillium Communications designed chips that let telephone companies deliver DSL broadband over ordinary copper phone lines.
lede: In 2000, most homes reached the internet through a dial-up modem. Telephone companies wanted to sell faster service without laying new cable, and DSL let them push broadband down the copper lines already running to every house. Centillium, based in Fremont, California, designed the chips that made DSL equipment work. It went public in May 2000, when the race to wire homes for broadband was at full speed.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Centillium bet that DSL would be the main way households got broadband, and that phone companies would buy huge amounts of equipment to offer it. Its chips went into the gear at the phone company's office and into some home modems. Large contracts in Japan, where DSL spread quickly, became a major source of revenue. It competed against much larger chip companies for these contracts.

sections.heading: Slower Lines
sections.body: Centillium priced its IPO at $19 a share in May 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. Its shares soared at first, then fell as telecom spending dropped and chip prices came down. The company tried to move into new areas such as voice-over-IP and fiber chips. In 2008 TranSwitch acquired Centillium. DSL itself went on to connect many millions of homes around the world.

cover.theme: electric light arrives (broadband down old wires)

dek: CoolSavings offered printable coupons and special offers online, paid for by the brands and retailers that wanted shoppers.
lede: For generations, Americans clipped coupons from Sunday newspapers. CoolSavings, based in Chicago, moved the coupon online. Members signed up, chose offers from brands and stores, and printed coupons at home. Advertisers paid CoolSavings for each shopper who saw or used an offer. The company went public in May 2000, just after internet stocks had begun to fall from their peak. Shoppers could browse offers by category and save their favorites.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: CoolSavings bet that coupons would be a strong lure for online shoppers and a precise tool for advertisers. Because members registered, the company knew who was using each offer. That data made it more valuable to brands than a scattered newspaper insert. The model, though, depended on online advertising budgets, which shrank sharply after 2000. It also collected detailed profiles from members who signed up. Those profiles let it target offers by place and interest.

sections.heading: A New Name
sections.body: CoolSavings priced its IPO at $7 a share in May 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. The dot-com crash cut its advertising revenue, and the company relied on investment from the media firm Landmark Communications to stay afloat. It later moved into broader online marketing and renamed itself Q Interactive. Landmark eventually sold the business to an investment firm. Its idea of digital coupons later became common on phones and store apps.

dek: HealthStream provides online training, credentialing and workforce software for hospitals and other health care organizations.
lede: Hospitals must train their staff constantly, from new safety rules to required certifications, and nurses on night shifts cannot easily attend a classroom. HealthStream, founded in Nashville in 1990, brought that training online. Its courses and tracking tools helped hospitals prove that staff had completed required learning. It went public in April 2000, during the dot-com era, as one of a wave of companies bringing health care onto the internet.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: HealthStream bet that hospitals would move required training onto the web and pay for it by subscription. Its platform delivered courses and kept records of who had completed what. Over time it added tools for scheduling, credentialing and measuring patient experience. Its focus on a single industry let it build deep relationships with hospital systems. Its customers range from small community hospitals to large health systems.

sections.heading: Steady Through the Years
sections.body: HealthStream priced its IPO at $9 a share in April 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. Its shares fell in the dot-com crash, but the company kept growing as hospitals adopted online learning. It expanded into workforce and credentialing software. HealthStream is still public, still based in Nashville, and trades as HSTM. It is one of the few health care internet companies of 2000 still operating independently.

cover.theme: a woman by the lamp (the night shift)

dek: Saba Software sold software that helped large organizations manage employee training, performance and talent.
lede: In the late 1990s, large companies spent heavily on employee training but had little idea what it achieved. Saba, founded in 1997 by Bobby Yazdani, built software to plan, deliver and track learning across an entire workforce. It went public in April 2000, as e-learning was one of the hottest ideas in business software and companies were moving training from classrooms to screens.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Saba bet that learning would become a managed business process, tied to each employee's skills and goals. Its learning management system let companies assign courses, track completion and link training to performance. Large corporations and government agencies were early customers. The company later widened its products to cover hiring, reviews and succession planning. Its customers included some of the largest companies and agencies in the world.

sections.heading: Out of the Spotlight
sections.body: Saba priced its IPO at $15 a share in April 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. The shares fell sharply in the crash, but the company survived and grew. In the early 2010s it faced an accounting scandal and restated years of results. In 2015 Vector Capital took Saba private, and in 2020 Cornerstone OnDemand bought it. Its name came from the ancient kingdom of Sheba.

cover.artwork: King Solomon Receiving the Queen of Sheba
cover.artist: Master of the Antwerp Adoration Group

dek: LivePerson makes chat and messaging software that lets companies talk with customers on websites and apps.
lede: In 2000, a shopper with a question on a website usually had to call a phone number or send an email and wait. LivePerson, founded by Robert LoCascio, put a chat button on the page so a real person could answer right away. Companies paid a monthly fee for each agent. It went public in April 2000, just weeks after the Nasdaq peak, with a product that few companies yet knew they needed.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: LivePerson bet that live conversation would help websites sell more and serve customers better. Its chat software was hosted, so companies could add it without new servers. Online retailers, banks and telecom companies became major customers. The company later moved from website chat to messaging across apps and channels, and added automated assistants. Its agents could handle several chats at once, which saved money for its clients.

sections.heading: Surviving the Silence
sections.body: LivePerson priced its IPO at $8 a share in April 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. Its shares fell below $1 in the crash, but the company cut costs and survived. It grew steadily through the 2000s and 2010s as online chat became normal. LivePerson is still public and trades as LPSN. It remains a pioneer of the chat window that now appears on so many websites.

dek: ARTISTdirect ran a music website with artist pages, news and merchandise, and backed a record label.
lede: In the late 1990s, musicians and fans were discovering each other online, and record labels were slow to follow. ARTISTdirect, founded in Los Angeles by music industry veterans, built a network of artist sites and a store for music and merchandise. It also launched a record label with well-known industry figures. The company went public in March 2000, as Napster was shaking the music business.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: ARTISTdirect bet that artists would want a direct line to their fans, and that a site built around them could earn money from merchandise, advertising and music sales. It gave musicians a share of what their fans spent. The idea was early. Fans were moving to free downloads, and online music sales were still years from catching on. Its artist pages offered news, tour dates and merchandise in one place.

sections.heading: Fading Out
sections.body: ARTISTdirect priced its IPO at $12 a share in March 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. Losses mounted as the dot-com market fell and the label struggled. The company cut back sharply and spent much of the decade searching for a stable business. It never regained the attention it had at its offering. Its early idea of a direct link between artists and fans became common on later platforms.

tagline: A Watchful Eye on the Wire
dek: Websense made web filtering software that let employers control and monitor which websites their staff could visit.
lede: When offices connected to the internet in the late 1990s, employers soon found staff browsing shopping, sports and worse during work hours. Websense, based in San Diego, built software that sat on a company's network and blocked or logged visits to sites by category. Its database classified millions of web pages. It went public in March 2000, as businesses rushed to put rules around their new internet connections.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Websense bet that every company with an internet connection would need a way to manage how it was used. It sold subscriptions to its constantly updated list of categorized sites. That recurring revenue made the business steady. Over time it moved into broader security, protecting against malware and data leaks as well as unwanted browsing. Schools and government agencies also became large customers.

sections.heading: Bought and Rebuilt
sections.body: Websense priced its IPO at $18 a share in March 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. It was one of the few offerings of that month to grow into a lasting business. In 2013 Thoma Bravo took Websense private for about $906 million. It later combined with Raytheon's cyber business and was renamed Forcepoint. The brand lives on in the security products that followed.

fate: Taken private by founder Robert Hammond, 2003
dek: PartsBase ran an online marketplace where airlines and repair shops searched for and bought aircraft parts.
lede: Keeping an airplane flying means finding the right part quickly, often from a supplier across the world. In the 1990s that search ran on phone calls and fax machines. PartsBase, based in Boca Raton, Florida, built a searchable online database of aviation parts listed by thousands of suppliers. It went public in March 2000, at the height of excitement about business-to-business marketplaces.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: PartsBase bet that the aviation parts trade would move onto a single shared marketplace. Buyers searched its listings and contacted sellers, and members paid subscription fees for access. The model fit a niche market where speed and accuracy mattered. It could not, though, match the lofty expectations set by the wider B2B boom. Its users included airlines, repair stations and parts dealers around the world.

sections.heading: Back to Private Hands
sections.body: PartsBase priced its IPO at $13 a share in March 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. Its shares fell steeply as the B2B bubble burst. The company kept serving aviation buyers and sellers. In 2003 founder Robert Hammond took PartsBase private, and it continued to operate as a private company. It was one of the few B2B marketplaces of its era to survive in some form.

dek: Caldera Systems sold a business version of the Linux operating system, along with support and training.
lede: In 1999 Linux was the darling of the technology world. Red Hat and VA Linux had both soared on their first days of trading, and investors wanted more. Caldera Systems, based in Orem, Utah, sold a polished Linux distribution aimed at businesses. It went public in March 2000, within days of the Nasdaq peak, and its shares jumped on the first day.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Caldera bet that businesses would pay for a supported, easy-to-install version of Linux, just as they paid for other operating systems. It offered training and services alongside its software. The company had roots in Novell's circle, and it aimed squarely at corporate networks. Its product line included both desktop and server versions of Linux. Its founders had worked at Novell before starting the company.

sections.heading: From Linux to Lawsuits
sections.body: Caldera priced its IPO at $14 a share in March 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. In 2001 it bought the Unix business of the Santa Cruz Operation and later renamed itself The SCO Group. SCO then sued IBM and others, claiming Linux used its Unix code. The lawsuits went badly, and SCO filed for bankruptcy in 2007. Its story became one of the strangest in the history of open source software.

dek: ImproveNet matched homeowners with screened contractors and architects for remodeling and repair projects.
lede: Finding a reliable contractor has always been a gamble based on word of mouth. ImproveNet, founded in 1996, tried to make it easier by building an online service that screened contractors and matched them with homeowners planning a project. Contractors paid for the leads. It went public in March 2000, one of many companies of the time promising to bring an old local trade onto the web.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: ImproveNet bet that homeowners would trust a website to vet contractors, and that contractors would pay for qualified leads. It checked licenses and references and offered tools to estimate project costs. The idea was sound, and later companies built large businesses on it. In 2000, though, too few homeowners were looking for contractors online. Its service covered projects from kitchen remodels to new roofs.

sections.heading: A Remodel of Its Own
sections.body: ImproveNet priced its IPO at $16 a share in March 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. Its shares fell steeply within months, and the company cut costs to survive. In 2002 it merged with eTechLogix, a private software firm based in Arizona, and new management took over. The combined company moved away from its original consumer focus. Its original idea was later proven by other home services sites.

dek: Loudeye encoded audio and video for online distribution and ran digital music stores for other companies.
lede: In the late 1990s, record labels and broadcasters had huge libraries of music and video, but almost none of it was ready for the internet. Loudeye, founded in Seattle in 1997, converted that media into digital formats and hosted it for streaming and download. It went public in March 2000, when streaming media was one of the most talked-about ideas on the web.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Loudeye bet that every media company would need to put its content online, and would rather hire a specialist than build the tools in-house. It digitized vast music catalogs and later built a platform that powered online music stores for retailers and mobile carriers. The company also bought OD2, a European digital music distributor. Its customers included record labels, radio stations and retailers.

sections.heading: Heard by Nokia
sections.body: Loudeye priced its IPO at $16 a share in March 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. Its shares fell sharply after the bubble burst, and it changed strategy several times. Its digital music platform caught the eye of Nokia, which was building a music service for its phones. In 2006 Nokia acquired Loudeye for about $60 million. The deal gave Nokia a ready-made music platform.

cover.artwork: The Seven Trumpets, from The Apocalypse

dek: Digitas was a Boston marketing agency that used data and digital channels to help large brands reach customers directly.
lede: Digitas began in 1980 as Bronner Slosberg Humphrey, a Boston direct-mail agency founded by Michael Bronner. By the late 1990s it had reinvented itself as a digital marketing firm, helping large companies use data to reach customers by mail, email and the web. It went public in March 2000, as big brands were scrambling to figure out how to market online.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Digitas bet that marketing would become more personal and measurable, and that big companies would need a partner to make sense of their customer data. It combined strategy, data analysis and creative work in one firm. Its clients included banks, telecom companies and car makers, and they spent heavily on its services. Its work blended the discipline of direct mail with the reach of the web.

sections.heading: Into a Global Network
sections.body: Digitas priced its IPO at $24 a share in March 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. Revenue fell in the downturn, but the company recovered as online advertising grew. It bought other agencies, including Modem Media. In 2007 Publicis Groupe acquired Digitas for about $1.3 billion, and it became a core part of Publicis's digital business. The Digitas name is still used by the agency today.

dek: Versata sold software that let companies build business applications by writing rules instead of traditional code.
lede: In 2000, businesses were rushing to put their operations onto the web, and programmers were scarce. Versata, based in the San Francisco Bay Area, offered a different way to build applications. Developers described business rules, such as how to calculate a price or approve an order, and Versata's software produced the working program. It went public in March 2000, at the very peak of the market.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Versata bet that business rules could be separated from code, which would let companies build and change applications faster. Its tools ran on popular Java application servers. The approach appealed to large companies with complex logic. Sales, however, depended on big projects, and those slowed sharply when tech budgets were cut. Its software was used for order processing, pricing and similar tasks.

sections.heading: Checkmate
sections.body: Versata priced its IPO at $24 a share in March 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. Its shares traded well above the offer price at first, then fell steeply as the market crashed. The company cut staff and shrank for several years. In 2006 Trilogy, the Austin software company, acquired Versata. Under Trilogy, the Versata name became an umbrella for many acquired software products.
